claims.text: product-search-requirements.md scope: in-shop search (app and web) is in scope; public product pages for search engines are out of scope, left by ADR 0017 to a separate decision, not re-decided there.

Scenarios TK-1..TK-5 with measures: no-diacritic words find Bàn phím cơ (seed); full matches before partial; only shop A's products; new/renamed found within minutes (assumed); search does not take ordering capacity, a measure with no number, response: ordering answers as on a normal day.
TK-4 is the same choice the product list already has in consistency-per-operation.md, the file setting per operation how stale a read may be: slightly stale is allowed.

claims.text: Estimate: at most a few thousand products per shop (assumed 5,000), a few hundred on average (assumed 200), about 200,000 rows across 1,000 shops, which the team judges PostgreSQL holds easily; searches assumed 20% of product reads, about 27/s of the plan's peak of about 133 reads/s.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/product-search-requirements.md @ stage-4 lines 38-44; docs/design/capacity-plan.md @ stage-4 line 24

claims.text: ProductCache, the Redis cache for products, keeps products one at a time by id; a search has no id to look up; the product list reads CatalogDbContext directly; every read and write goes to the primary PostgreSQL, where orders are also written.

claims.text: Ranked drivers in product-search-requirements.md: (1) no-diacritic words find the product (TK-1); (2) search never takes capacity orders need (TK-5); (3) results only in the caller's shop (TK-3).
The assumptions table names the product owner as the one who confirms 'at most 5,000 products per shop' and 'found after a few minutes is enough'.
ADR 0017 leaves public product pages for search engines to a separate ADR; the HTML the Flutter app sends for a product page holds no product name.
SQL = on text compares the whole string: WHERE name = 'ban phim' does not match 'Bàn phím cơ'; ORDER BY id returns rows in id order, not by how well they match.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: Functions and Operators > Comparison Operators; Character Types / Collation (deterministic collations)

claims.text: Framing in-shop search as ranked scenarios with measures is preferable when customers type real words with or without diacritics; a plain ?name= filter can be enough when names are exact codes customers copy; one 'search' covering search engines fits only after the separate ADR exists.

'Within minutes' lets search read a copy updated later, 'at once' ties it to the products table, so it leaves fewer options; ask for it only when a late result has a measurable cost; recording 'minutes, assumed' with its confirmer keeps it cheap to revisit.

Choices: exact part codes may make an exact-match scenario the whole requirement; an instant-freshness demand needs a measurable loss before replacing TK-4; 500,000 products per shop breaks the estimate's assumption, so redo it before designing.

A ?name= equality filter added to the product list reads the table on the primary on every call with no cache, so a saved rename is visible on the next request (passes TK-4); the list at stage-4 takes no shop parameter.
